title: Distributional Semantics & the Vector-Space View
oneLineScope: Meaning from co-occurrence — the vector-space view of words, from Firth and Harris.
prose:
Where we are. This is one of the two entry points into the tutorial — you arrive here directly from the introduction, with no prior node as a formal prerequisite. That is deliberate. Distributional semantics is your home turf: the Harris–Firth tradition, co-occurrence matrices, Latent Semantic Analysis. This node does not re-teach you that material; it uses it as the bridge. The vector-space view of meaning that you already know is the same conceptual foundation the transformer era is built on — the machinery changes, the core idea does not. Starting here means the rest of the tutorial is a recognizable extension of something you already understand, not a foreign import.

The gist. Distributional semantics operationalizes the principle that a word’s meaning can be read off from the statistical company it keeps. Build a matrix whose rows are words and whose columns are the contexts they appear in; fill it with weighted co-occurrence counts. Now two words are semantically similar when their row vectors point in the same direction — cosine similarity in that space is an empirical measure of semantic relatedness. Apply truncated SVD to compress and denoise the matrix (Latent Semantic Analysis), and you get compact, dense representations that generalize across synonymy without a single human annotation. This is the count-and-factorize pipeline, and it is the direct conceptual ancestor of the learned embeddings that every transformer takes as input.

Why it matters. Word embeddings and attention are not departures from distributional semantics — they are its continuation by other means. Tracing the lineage from this node forward makes every subsequent architectural choice legible as a change of machinery rather than a change of ideas. It also puts one central limitation in sharp relief: count-based methods commit to a single vector per word type, averaging over all the contexts that type ever appears in. That conflation is the problem contextual representations — and ultimately attention — exist to solve.

From the hypothesis to a matrix

Zellig Harris stated the principle in 1954: morphemes that appear in similar distributions of surrounding contexts tend to be semantically related. John Rupert Firth sharpened it three years later into its most quoted form: “You shall know a word by the company it keeps.” For the following four decades, this was the primary computational theory of how meaning could be extracted from unannotated text.

The concrete realization is the term–context matrix. Take a vocabulary of \(V\) word types as the rows and a set of context tokens or windows as the columns. For each pair \((w_i, c_j)\), record how many times \(w_i\) appears in a window containing \(c_j\). Each row is then the word’s co-occurrence profile — a vector in \(\mathbb{R}^V\) recording how it distributes itself across contexts. Words with similar distributions get similar row vectors, and cosine similarity between those rows is the operational measure of semantic relatedness.

Take bank as the canonical example: it appears near deposit, loan, and interest in financial documents and near river, erodes, and current in geographical ones. Its row vector therefore sits between a finance cluster and a nature cluster in the space — the polysemy is encoded structurally as a mix of two distributional signatures, but not resolved. That unresolved conflation is the load-bearing limitation, and we will return to it.

Weighting the matrix: PPMI

Raw counts are a poor choice for cell values. Very frequent words like the and of co-occur with almost everything, so they dominate every row and swamp genuine semantic signal. The standard remedy is Pointwise Mutual Information (PMI):

\[ \text{PMI}(w, c) = \log_2 \frac{p(w, c)}{p(w)\,p(c)} \]

Here \(p(w, c)\) is the joint probability of the pair — the fraction of all observed \((w, c)\) pairs in the corpus — and \(p(w)\), \(p(c)\) are the marginals. High PMI means the word and context co-occur more than their independent frequencies would predict: a clean information-theoretic measure of specificity. The practical variant is PPMI (Positive PMI), which floors negative values at zero, since negative associations are statistically unreliable in sparse matrices. The PPMI matrix is far more discriminating than raw counts.

Dimensionality reduction: LSA as truncated SVD

Even a well-weighted co-occurrence matrix is enormous — \(V \times V\) with \(V\) in the hundreds of thousands — extremely sparse, and noisy from idiosyncratic pairings. The natural next step, immediately recognizable from factor analysis, is low-rank approximation. Apply truncated SVD to the PPMI matrix \(M\):

\[ M \approx U_k \Sigma_k V_k^{\top} \]

where \(U_k \in \mathbb{R}^{V \times k}\), \(\Sigma_k \in \mathbb{R}^{k \times k}\) (diagonal, non-negative), and \(V_k^{\top} \in \mathbb{R}^{k \times V}\), with \(k \ll V\) (typically 100–300). The rows of \(U_k \Sigma_k\) become the dense, low-dimensional word representations. This is precisely Latent Semantic Analysis (LSA), introduced by Deerwester et al. in 1990 for information retrieval.

From a factor-analytic perspective, LSA discovers the latent dimensions of meaning that best reconstruct the observed co-occurrence patterns — the principal components, in effect, of the PPMI matrix. The compression serves two ends simultaneously: it discards noise (rare, idiosyncratic co-occurrences are absorbed by the small singular values that get dropped) and it induces generalization (words that share many context neighbors end up close in the low-rank space even if they never directly co-occurred). Harris’s distributional equivalence relation, stated as a linguistic principle, turns out to be captured by the dominant singular structure of the co-occurrence matrix.

What counting cannot do

The count-and-factorize pipeline works, but it carries three liabilities that motivate everything that comes next.

Sparsity. Most \((w, c)\) pairs never appear in any finite corpus, so most matrix entries are zero. PPMI helps at the margins, but rare words have unreliable profiles regardless of weighting.

Static conflation. Each word type gets one vector — a single point in \(\mathbb{R}^k\) that averages over all its contexts. Bank in “river bank” and bank in “central bank” are forced to share the same row. Polysemy is smeared, not modeled. This is not a failure of Harris’s hypothesis; it is a failure of the one-vector-per-type commitment. The hypothesis says meaning is constituted by distributional patterns; it says nothing about collapsing those patterns into a single point.

Scale and coupling. Assembling, weighting, and factorizing a \(V \times V\) PPMI matrix is expensive at large \(V\), and the resulting vectors sit awkwardly in gradient-based downstream systems: their dimensionality is tied to the corpus vocabulary, not freely learned end-to-end.

Where it leads

The neural approach does not abandon the distributional hypothesis — it intensifies it. Word2vec and GloVe, the subject of the next node, still learn from co-occurrence patterns; they simply replace the count-then-factorize pipeline with a prediction objective trained by gradient descent. The resulting dense vectors — embeddings — are not explicitly SVD factors, but Levy & Goldberg (2014) showed that skip-gram with negative sampling implicitly factorizes a shifted PMI matrix, closing the theoretical loop directly back to Harris and Firth.

The deeper shift comes later still. Transformer-era models make representations contextual: rather than committing to one vector per word type, the model computes a fresh representation for each token occurrence, conditioned on the full surrounding sequence. Scaled dot-product attention is the mechanism that does that conditioning — a differentiable, content-addressed lookup that finally lets the system distinguish bank the institution from bank the landform at inference time. The Firth intuition survives intact across sixty years of development; what changes, node by node, is the granularity and power with which it is applied.

diagrams.caption: The distributional hypothesis in action: the same target word 'bank' shown in three sentence contexts, each contributing a different set of neighbors, building up the word's distributional signature.
diagrams.altText: The word bank sits in a central box labeled target word. Three context windows radiate outward, each showing a short token sequence with bank highlighted: context A shows river bank erodes with neighbors river and erodes labeled in green; context B shows deposit bank teller with neighbors deposit and teller labeled in blue; context C shows bank lends money with neighbors lends and money labeled in blue. Arrows from each context point to the center. A box on the right labeled distributional signature of bank accumulates the neighbors from all contexts, with a note that the co-occurrence vector captures both senses and that static vectors conflate them.
diagrams.prompt: Conceptual diagram illustrating the distributional hypothesis. Center: a box labeled 'bank' with subtitle 'target word'. Three context-window boxes radiate outward (upper-left, mid-left, lower-left), each showing a short token sequence — context A: [river] [bank] [erodes]; context B: [deposit] [bank] [teller]; context C: [bank] [lends] [money] — with the 'bank' token lightly shaded to mark it as the target and the surrounding neighbor tokens labeled. Each context box has a small label reading its distinctive neighbors (context A neighbors: river, erodes; context B neighbors: deposit, teller; context C neighbors: lends, money). Arrows from each context box point toward the central 'bank' box. On the right, a box labeled 'distributional signature of bank' lists the accumulated neighbor types and ends with a note: 'static vector conflates both senses — attention later resolves per-context.' Include the Firth quote at the bottom: 'You shall know a word by the company it keeps. — Firth, 1957'. No equations; purely conceptual.

bibliography.citation: Harris, Z. S. (1954). Distributional Structure. Word, 10(2–3), 146–162.
bibliography.annotation: The founding paper. Harris states the distributional hypothesis as a linguistic principle and defines it operationally in terms of substitutability in contexts. Read this for the intellectual origin of the entire vector-space approach to semantics; the argument is linguistic, not computational, but it is the bedrock everything else rests on.

bibliography.citation: Deerwester, S., Dumais, S. T., Furnas, G. W., Landauer, T. K., & Harshman, R. (1990). Indexing by Latent Semantic Analysis. Journal of the American Society for Information Science, 41(6), 391–407.
bibliography.annotation: The LSA paper. Introduces truncated SVD of a term–document matrix as a way to extract latent semantic structure for information retrieval. §2–3 cover the matrix construction and SVD; §4 gives the retrieval experiments. The place to go for the mathematical details of the count-then-factorize approach.

bibliography.citation: Firth, J. R. (1957). A synopsis of linguistic theory 1930–1955. In Studies in Linguistic Analysis (pp. 1–32). Blackwell.
bibliography.annotation: The source of the famous dictum. The broader essay is a statement of Firth's contextual theory of meaning; the distributional hypothesis is one instantiation of it. Worth reading for the original framing, which is more nuanced than the soundbite suggests.

bibliography.citation: Jurafsky, D., & Martin, J. H. Speech and Language Processing (3rd ed., draft), Chapter 6: Vector Semantics and Embeddings.
bibliography.annotation: The best practitioner-level treatment of the path from co-occurrence matrices through PPMI and LSA to word2vec. §6.1–6.5 cover the count-based foundations; §6.6–6.8 the transition to neural embeddings. The notation is clean and the worked examples are useful. The chapter to read alongside both this node and the word-embeddings node.
